title: Hypercalcemia: PTH, PTHrP and Albumin-Adjusted Calcium
summary: Use intact PTH to separate primary hyperparathyroidism from PTH-independent hypercalcemia such as PTHrP-mediated malignancy, explain how PTH raises calcium, and apply albumin adjustment with its limits.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 16 Hits 1–4 (first lesson for Ch. 16). Checked against Kochman 2023 (PHPT, Fifth International Workshop), Mirrakhimov 2015 (hypercalcemia of malignancy) and Desgagnés 2025 (albumin-adjusted calcium). Correction: the reviewer’s corrected-calcium formula uses a 4.4 g/dL reference albumin; the commonly used simplified Payne formula uses 4.0 g/dL (rv-calcium-ref-albumin). Not taught: “together 80–90% of cases” (Hit 1), urinary cAMP and “PTHrP elevated in 50–90%” (Hit 3) — not in the sources read.

objectives: Describe the three ways PTH raises serum calcium.
Use intact PTH to separate PTH-dependent from PTH-independent hypercalcemia.
Calculate albumin-adjusted calcium and state its limitations.

scenes.title: Two high calciums, opposite PTH
scenes.altText: Two invented chemistry reports. Patient 1: outpatient, mild symptoms, total calcium 11.0 mg/dL, intact PTH high-normal/elevated, phosphate low-normal. Patient 2: inpatient with lung cancer, confused, calcium 14.2 mg/dL, intact PTH suppressed. A third slip: total calcium 8.0 mg/dL with albumin 2.0 g/dL. Question token: “What drives each calcium — and is the third one really low?”

cues.text: Two patients have high calcium. One is an outpatient with calcium of 11, a high-normal to elevated PTH and low-normal phosphate.
The other has lung cancer, confusion, calcium above 14, and a suppressed PTH. A third patient has total calcium of 8 with albumin of only 2.
What drives each calcium, and is the third one really low?

props.label: What drives each? Is #3 really low?

scenes.title: How PTH raises calcium
scenes.altText: PTH card (Kochman 2023): PTH (1) increases bone resorption, (2) increases renal calcium reabsorption and suppresses renal phosphate reabsorption, and (3) indirectly increases intestinal calcium absorption by stimulating conversion of 25(OH)D to 1,25(OH)₂D in the proximal tubule. Feedback token: high calcium normally suppresses PTH via the calcium-sensing receptor. Measurement card: albumin is the major (not the only) calcium carrier; ionized calcium can be measured directly and may be preferred (Mirrakhimov 2015).

cues.text: Parathyroid hormone raises calcium three ways. It increases bone resorption.
It makes the kidney reabsorb more calcium while excreting more phosphate.
And, indirectly, it raises intestinal calcium absorption by stimulating the kidney to make active vitamin D, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.
Normally, a high calcium switches PTH off. And because much calcium rides on albumin, a low albumin lowers total calcium; ionized calcium can be measured directly.

scenes.title: PTH-driven vs PTH-independent
scenes.altText: Two branches. PTH-dependent: primary hyperparathyroidism — most common cause of hypercalcemia in the general population; diagnosed by elevated albumin-adjusted calcium with elevated or inappropriately high intact PTH, twice ≥ 2 weeks apart; phosphate usually low-normal (Kochman 2023). PTH-independent (PTH suppressed): hypercalcemia of malignancy — PTHrP-mediated humoral hypercalcemia ≈ 80%, osteolytic metastases ≈ 20% (breast cancer, myeloma), 1,25(OH)₂D-mediated (some lymphomas), rarely ectopic PTH; usually more severe and symptomatic; granulomatous diseases (sarcoidosis, TB) via 1,25(OH)₂D (Mirrakhimov 2015). Rule: in hypercalcemia, a high-normal PTH is inappropriate and points to parathyroid hyperfunction.

cues.text: First branch: PTH-dependent. Primary hyperparathyroidism is the most common cause of high calcium in the general population. The diagnosis is a raised albumin-adjusted calcium with an elevated or inappropriately normal PTH, on two occasions at least two weeks apart.
In hypercalcemia, even a high-normal PTH is inappropriate: it should be suppressed. Phosphate is usually low-normal.

Second branch: PTH suppressed. In malignancy, about 80 percent of hypercalcemia is caused by PTH-related protein, PTHrP, while the patient’s own PTH is suppressed. About 20 percent comes from bone-destroying metastases, mostly breast cancer and myeloma.

Other PTH-independent causes include tumours or granulomatous diseases, such as sarcoidosis and tuberculosis, that make active vitamin D. Malignant hypercalcemia is usually more severe and symptomatic.

scenes.title: Adjusting for albumin — and its limits
scenes.altText: Formula card: commonly used simplified Payne formula — adjusted Ca (mg/dL) = total Ca + 0.8 × (4.0 − albumin g/dL), i.e., mmol/L + 0.02 × (40 − albumin g/L) (Desgagnés 2025; Mirrakhimov 2015). Worked example: 8.0 + 0.8 × (4.0 − 2.0) = 9.6 mg/dL. Evidence card (Desgagnés 2025, n > 20,000 paired results): unadjusted total calcium correlated with ionized calcium at least as well as the adjusted value and agreed better in classifying hypo-/normo-/hypercalcemia → measure ionized calcium when it matters. Back to the hook: Patient 1 → PTH-dependent, likely PHPT; Patient 2 → PTH suppressed with cancer, likely PTHrP (humoral); Patient 3 → adjusted ≈ 9.6 (normal) — confirm with ionized calcium.

cues.text: The commonly used simplified formula adds 0.8 milligrams per decilitre for every gram per decilitre that albumin falls below 4.0.
For the third patient: 8.0 plus 0.8 times 2, which is 9.6, within the usual reference range.
But adjustment is imperfect. In a large 2025 study, unadjusted total calcium matched ionized calcium at least as well as the adjusted value. When it matters, measure ionized calcium.
Back to the patients: patient one has PTH-dependent hypercalcemia, most likely primary hyperparathyroidism.
Patient two has suppressed PTH with cancer, most likely PTH-related protein. Patient three probably has normal calcium; confirm with ionized calcium.

props.label: Adjusted ≠ ionized: measure iCa if it matters

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A normal PTH rules out hyperparathyroidism in hypercalcemia” (✓ high-normal PTH with high calcium is inappropriate → PHPT); “Malignancy hypercalcemia shows a high PTH” (✓ PTH is suppressed; PTHrP or other mechanisms); “Adjusted calcium equals ionized calcium” (✓ adjustment is imperfect; measure ionized calcium).

cues.text: Trap one: a normal PTH rules out hyperparathyroidism. With high calcium, PTH should be suppressed, so a high-normal value is inappropriate and points to primary hyperparathyroidism.
Trap two: cancer-related hypercalcemia shows high PTH. Usually PTH is suppressed, and the culprit is PTH-related protein, bone metastases, or active vitamin D.
Trap three: albumin-adjusted calcium equals ionized calcium. It does not reliably; measure ionized calcium when classification matters.

scenes.title: Ask PTH first
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Ask PTH first: if PTH talks (high or normal) it’s the gland; if PTH is silent, look for the tumour or the vitamin.” Tokens: PTH talks → PHPT · PTH silent → PTHrP / mets / 1,25-D · Albumin low → ionized Ca. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: ask PTH first. If PTH talks, high or normal, it is the gland. If PTH is silent, look for the tumour or the vitamin.

Where it breaks: cancer patients can also have primary hyperparathyroidism; rare cancers make PTH itself; and medications or other conditions such as familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia need separate consideration.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “PTH ↑ or inappropriately normal + Ca ↑ → PHPT (most common overall) · PTH suppressed → malignancy (PTHrP ≈ 80%, osteolytic ≈ 20%), 1,25-D, granuloma”, “Adjusted Ca = Ca + 0.8 × (4.0 − albumin) — imperfect; ionized Ca is preferred”.

cues.text: In hypercalcemia, read PTH first: a raised or inappropriately normal PTH means primary hyperparathyroidism, a suppressed PTH points to PTHrP-mediated malignancy or other causes, and albumin adjustment never replaces ionized calcium.

props.label: PTH ↑/normal + Ca ↑ → PHPT · PTH ↓ → PTHrP (≈ 80%), mets, 1,25-D
Adjusted Ca = Ca + 0.8 × (4.0 − alb): imperfect → ionized Ca

explanation.what: Plain language: when blood calcium is high, the first question is whether the parathyroid glands are driving it (PTH high or not switched off) or something else is (PTH switched off), such as a tumour hormone; and because calcium travels on albumin, a low albumin can make total calcium look falsely low. Scientific terms: intact PTH, PTH-related protein (PTHrP), primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT), humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy, osteolytic metastases, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, albumin-adjusted (corrected) calcium, ionized calcium.
explanation.why: PTH increases bone resorption, renal calcium reabsorption with phosphate excretion, and (via 1,25(OH)₂D) intestinal absorption. High calcium normally suppresses PTH, so a non-suppressed PTH indicates autonomous parathyroid secretion. In PTH-independent causes such as tumour PTHrP, osteolysis or excess 1,25(OH)₂D, the high calcium suppresses native PTH.
explanation.measure: PHPT: elevated albumin-adjusted calcium with elevated or inappropriately high intact PTH, twice ≥ 2 weeks apart; phosphate usually low-normal (Kochman 2023). Malignancy: PTHrP ≈ 80%, osteolytic ≈ 20%, also 1,25-D-mediated and rare ectopic PTH; PTH suppressed or low-normal (Mirrakhimov 2015). Adjusted Ca (mg/dL) = Ca + 0.8 × (4.0 − albumin g/dL); unadjusted total calcium agreed with ionized calcium at least as well (Desgagnés 2025).
explanation.differs: PTH-dependent (PHPT; PTH high/inappropriately normal) vs PTH-independent (PTHrP, osteolytic, vitamin D-mediated; PTH suppressed); total vs albumin-adjusted vs ionized calcium.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: interpreting PTH with high calcium, PTHrP in malignancy, PTH actions, and a corrected-calcium calculation (check which reference albumin the exam uses).

questions.stem: A patient has calcium 11.2 mg/dL (high) on two occasions three weeks apart and an intact PTH of 58 pg/mL (within the reference interval). What is the most likely cause?

options.rationale: Correct. With hypercalcemia, PTH should be suppressed; a normal PTH is inappropriately high.

options.text: No parathyroid problem because PTH is normal
options.rationale: Incorrect. A normal PTH is not appropriate when calcium is high.
Incorrect. Granulomatous disease raises calcium via 1,25(OH)₂D and suppresses PTH.

questions.stem: Total calcium is 7.6 mg/dL with albumin 2.0 g/dL. Using adjusted Ca = Ca + 0.8 × (4.0 − albumin), what is the adjusted calcium?

options.rationale: Incorrect. That is the unadjusted value.
Incorrect. That uses a 4.4 g/dL reference albumin (7.6 + 0.8 × 2.4 ≈ 9.5).
Incorrect. The correction is 0.8 per g/dL, not 2.0.

questions.stem: Which mechanism accounts for most hypercalcemia in patients with cancer?

options.rationale: Correct. PTHrP accounts for about 80% of malignancy-related hypercalcemia.
Incorrect. Osteolytic metastases account for about 20%.
Incorrect. Ectopic PTH production is rare.
Incorrect. Tumour-related 1,25(OH)₂D production occurs (e.g., some lymphomas) but is not the main mechanism.
